body.text: In short:
More than 20,000 properties have lost power on South Australia's Eyre Peninsula, with wild weather knocking over transmission towers in the region.
It is unclear when power will be restored, and phone services have also been impacted.
SA cabinet's emergency management committee will meet tonight.
Multiple electricity transmission towers have been brought down by storms, leaving more than 20,000 properties on South Australia's Eyre Peninsula without power.

Electricity supply was cut to more than 24,000 properties amid lightning storms this afternoon, and ElectraNet — which is responsible for transmission lines — has indicated it is unclear when power will be restored.
"Significant storm activity brought down transmission towers on the Eyre Peninsula, impacting electricity supply to customers south and west of Whyalla," it said in a statement.
"Power is unlikely to be restored in the immediate term, and our first step is to safely assess the damage and then determine the quickest and safest way to restore services for customers."
Phone services on the peninsula also appear to have been impacted, with residents in the region reporting communication challenges.
Wharminda farmer Chris Prime told ABC Radio Drive that two transmission towers, including one on his property, had been knocked down in storms and gusty winds.
"It's taken a couple of the large transmission lines down," he said.
"It looks like someone got angry and just crushed them up and pushed them over and laid them on the ground.
"There are two laying flat on the ground and a third one where the top third of it that carries the lines is just snapped over."
Mr Prime said the towers had been put up "only two or three years ago" and were about "25 or 30 metres tall".
"They carry the main power from Whyalla straight down to [Port] Lincoln," he said.
"Looking at the damage around it, in a line around it with trees down, there were wind, hail and rain in one hit. They weren't hit by lightning — I'm pretty sure it was just a good old wind blast."
Mr Prime was forced to stop reaping when the weather worsened and said the impact had been devastating.
"I don't like to have a guess, but I'm pretty confident that it's 100 per cent wiped out our crops," he said.
The situation has prompted a meeting of SA cabinet's emergency management committee, which will begin at 7pm tonight.
"Initial advice is that storm activity may have damaged parts of ElectraNet's transmission network, causing the outages," SA Premier Peter Malinauskas tweeted.
"I've spoken with the Acting Commissioner of Police, and we're continuing to monitor the situation closely.
"State government agencies stand ready to support affected communities."
As at 6pm, Telstra's website shows outages impacting the 4G network around the Port Lincoln area, with residents also reporting communication issues.
"Our technicians are attempting to establish temporary backup power or on-site fixes to restore services," it said just before 6pm today.
The telco said a "power fault" was to blame for the outage.
Port Lincoln's Hotel Boston venue manager, Nick Carlson, said its kitchen was forced to close because of the power outage.
"[Can probably last without power] until midnight … We'll reassess at midnight and see what we can do then," he said.
He said the fridges were filled full of food and could mean a big loss if the lights do not come back on.
'We've got a big weekend coming up so … the fridges are stocked, multiple fridges full of food, you know, live, fresh fish, meat, everything. So yeah, really hoping it doesn't get to that."
'Lightning has struck twice'
In 2016, as a result of the statewide blackout, parts of Eyre Peninsula were left without power for about three days.
Kimba Mayor Dean Johnson said it was unclear when power would be restored.

"They're estimating it will be back on about 9pm but from past history and experience, I'd say there's often an initial estimate and once they get up here and assess where the damage is and begin that process we might get an update from there," he said.
"I certainly hope it's not a repeat of the three-day outage we had many years ago, but it does seem the EP has been wiped out again."
The blackout has again raised the question of South Australia's energy security.
Mr Johnson said that in the aftermath of the 2016 event there were discussions about ensuring supply through back-up systems.
"What we were told hasn't eventuated and unfortunately it looks like lightning has struck twice," he said.
In a statement, SA Power Networks — which manages distribution — said the blackout was "connected to a possible lightning strike on the ElectraNet transmission network".
In its latest statement, ElectraNet said crews were "assessing the damage and working on a safe restoration plan".
"Safely restoring transmission services to the region is our highest priority," it said.
"We recognise this is a significant outage for communities and understand the disruption it is causing. We will continue to provide updates as further information becomes available.
"We ask the community to take extra care around storm-damaged areas, stay well clear of fallen or damaged powerlines and always assume fallen powerlines are live."
Ceduna Mayor Ken Maynard said the power went out in the West Coast town about 2pm.
"Various businesses have their own back-up supply after the big blackout 10 years ago," he said.
The region is prime grain growing country and Mr Maynard said the occurrence of the power outage during the "biggest harvest ever known in this area" would delay deliveries.

"At the moment, I believe, the biggest impact would be on the grain receivals in Thevenard. They can't receive grain when the power is out so they send the trucks back out to the bunkers, out to the east of Ceduna," he said.
"That will slow the process of delivering down quite considerably, which will cause frustrations all round.
"We're in the middle of the biggest harvest ever known in this area — it's just huge. The amount of grain coming in is just phenomenal."
